author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Indonesia produced the world’s highest fire-related carbon dioxide emissions during the first week of September as wildfires burned through drought-stricken forest and peatland on Borneo and Sumatra.

Fire Emissions Watch, developed by the European Union’s Copernicus climate service, estimated 19.7 million metric tons from September 1 through September 7. That was more than one-third of the global total and 273% above Indonesia’s seasonal average, though below the same week in the severe 2015 fire year.

Authorities described the current season as the country’s most intense in 11 years. More than 13,000 hotspots were recorded from August 1 through September 8. In Pontianak, West Kalimantan, the air-quality index reached 394 on Wednesday; readings above 300 are considered hazardous.

The emergency remains developing because El Niño-driven heat and drought can sustain fires into October. Satellite estimates may also miss low-temperature or underground peat fires. Later field assessments will be needed to measure burned area, health effects and cross-border haze, while current air-quality readings can vary by place and hour.
dek: Satellite-based estimates put Indonesia’s fire emissions at 19.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide from September 1–7 as drought fuels a severe season.
headline: Indonesia wildfire emissions rise to world’s highest
